messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The night of the fire, Marcus was on the phone with his younger brother, Leo. He heard the crash first, then the shouting, then the wet, percussive sound of a body hitting the floor. He listened, frozen, as Leo’s girlfriend screamed and the sirens began to wail. He could not move from his couch; he could only hear his brother’s breathing stop. That was eighteen months ago. Leo survived, but Marcus has not. The memory lives in him not as a story he can tell, but as a series of snapshots—photographic, still, and silent—that slide into his mind without warning. When he tries to explain what happened, the words fail him; the event exists only in images and in the acrid, metallic smell of smoke and blood that sometimes fills his nostrils for no reason he can identify. He has come to believe that his own body is betraying him, that these reactions mean he is still in danger, even when he knows, logically, that the fire is long over.

Marcus is twenty-one, married, and unemployed. He used to work as a stock clerk in a grocery warehouse, but he stopped going after a co-worker made a passing comment about how dangerous family life could be. That single remark sent him home shaking, and he never returned. Now, any comment about family—whether on television, in a song, or overheard in a café—feels like a threat directed at him. He has become hypervigilant to the way people move. A sudden gesture from his wife, a stranger reaching into a pocket, a car braking too quickly—each one puts him immediately on guard. He cannot sleep. Most nights he lies awake, replaying the images, waiting for something else to happen. He is certain that if he lets his guard down, something terrible will strike again, and he will not be able to protect anyone.

Because he cannot trust his own vigilance, he has developed a set of rules to keep himself safe. He avoids all media that might depict violence or accidents—no crime shows, no news, no movies with sirens. He cannot bear to be alone in the apartment, so his wife has rearranged her work schedule to be home more often, a change that has strained their finances and their marriage. When the pressure inside him becomes unbearable, he cuts his forearms with a razor blade; the physical pain, he says, is the only thing that stops the images from cycling. But the self-harm also brings the memory back more vividly—the smell of smoke always returns afterward, and the photographic images flash more intensely for hours. He has found that the more he avoids, the more the memories intrude, and the more he feels he cannot rely on himself to cope.

His wife has started to notice that he flinches when she walks into a room too quickly. He knows this hurts her, but he cannot stop it. The threat he perceives in sudden movements is immediate and overwhelming, and it drives him deeper into avoidance. He has begun to believe that he is no longer capable of the things that used to define him—being a reliable partner, a protective older brother, a steady worker. He sees himself as broken, and that belief makes him scan the world even more anxiously for signs of danger. A person acting suspiciously on the street, a comment about family from a stranger, a glimpse of a burned hand or a scarred arm—each trigger confirms his appraisal that the world is unsafe and he is unequal to it. He has not visited Leo in the hospital since the first week. He cannot bear to see his brother’s scars. The sight of those specific body parts—the mottled skin on Leo’s forearm—would send him into a flashback so vivid he might believe he is back in that moment, listening to the phone line go dead.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a night last week when his wife found him standing in the bathroom, razor in hand, unable to speak. She told him she was afraid to leave him alone. He realized then that his fear of being alone had created the very thing he feared most: he could not be trusted by the person he loved. He is terrified that the memories will never stop, that he will never feel safe again, and that his marriage will not survive his silence. But he is also desperate enough to try anything. He wants to know if there is a way to put the fire out.
